# Data, Knowledge, and Representation {#sec-data-representations-world-models}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world."
>
> — Ludwig Wittgenstein, *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* [@Wittgenstein1922Tractatus, sec. 5.6]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What does an AI-native design system need to know, where does that information come from, and how should it be represented?*

**Core thesis:** *Architecture data is expensive, heterogeneous, and sparse; representation choices dictate what design relationships remain visible and determine what automated methods can discover or miss.*
:::

A Verilog module that passes linting can still deadlock an interconnect protocol, exceed its power-density limit, or miss timing at the required corner. In software engineering, code repositories give language models abundant examples of syntax; in computer architecture, syntax is the cheapest part of the problem. Useful architectural data has to couple structural choices to physical behavior, energy cost, and the operating conditions under which those observations were obtained.

Starting from a concrete architectural question, this chapter traces the data required across the hardware–software stack, from compiler intermediate representations (IRs) down to placed netlists, parasitic extractions, and signoff timing reports. Public code is plentiful, but a physically meaningful observation requires running the right workload through the right tools, and that is where hardware data becomes scarce. How a team represents, curates, and versions those observations determines what an automated design loop can learn from them and propose.

Raw observations become reusable architectural knowledge only when an explanation establishes why a design behaved as it did and where that conclusion holds. Every task-specific representation highlights the relationships a generator, predictor, or optimizer needs while leaving other physical effects out of view (@fig-ch04-cover-map). A congestion map derived from a placed design, for example, says nothing about IR drop, so the representation has to declare that omission and keep a link back to the layout and libraries it came from. This chapter examines these representation choices alongside restrictions on using and sharing the resulting data, defining the structured state required to run the Formulate and Explore stages of the life cycle introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology.

![**Representations expose target properties while creating architectural blind spots.** A source-linked project record supplies raw design data, from which task-specific representations project state for generation, prediction, or optimization. Because every projection abstracts away details, explicit schemas must declare unmodeled physical effects and preserve provenance back to authoritative design sources. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/ch04-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch04-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which a source-linked project record feeds a task-specific representation that exposes some properties while declaring blind spots and retaining provenance."}

## Data Requirements for AI-Native Design

When a team first builds an architectural dataset or prompts a generative model, the easiest files to gather are isolated source files and flat summary tables: a directory of Verilog modules, a spreadsheet of simulator cycle counts, or a collection of synthesis area reports. Feeding those unlinked files into a predictor or generator quickly breaks down in practice. A synthesized netlist that closed timing under a relaxed clock period in one technology library looks identical in raw Verilog to one that failed under tight constraints, and a simulator cycle count means nothing if the compiler tiling schedule and memory-traffic assumptions that produced it were never recorded. Training a surrogate or steering an automated search on such disconnected records teaches the model to chase spurious correlations across mismatched baselines.

To prevent those mismatches and support the life-cycle stages in @sec-architecture-20-ontology, an AI-native design system needs information across three connected dimensions: what the computation is supposed to do and what functional constraints it must obey, measurements that tie architectural choices to physical outcomes, and verifiable execution state that explains why one alternative outperforms another. A single architectural decision touches software compiler IRs, simulator execution traces, technology-mapped netlists, and physical signoff reports.

Because a decision spans all of those files, the central representation problem is deciding what counts as one evaluated example. For a kernel-latency predictor, a sample pairs an operator shape and compiler schedule with a neural processing unit (NPU) configuration and its cycle-accurate execution latency, whereas for a register-transfer level (RTL) generator, an example pairs an interface specification with synthesizable modules and vacuity-checked assertions. A *representation* converts these raw engineering artifacts into a structured mathematical form that computational methods can manipulate [@BengioEtAl2013RepresentationLearning], whether as discrete abstract syntax trees, control-data flow graphs, or learned embedding vectors. Turning these heterogeneous files into an executable workflow requires a pipeline that organizes raw design collateral into checked datasets and linked representations without breaking ties to the original design files (@fig-architecture-data-progression), so that each view preserves the physical and functional properties required for downstream checks while dropping details irrelevant to the active decision.

![**Architectural sources support different tasks through linked datasets, knowledge, and representations.** Raw design files and tool logs separate into durable project knowledge versus live candidate state before projecting into native, structured, or learned views. Source identity, versions, and tool environments remain persistently linked across the handoff so that derived views never displace native artifacts as the authoritative source of record. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-architecture-data-progression){#fig-architecture-data-progression width="100%" fig-alt="Flow diagram in which a left-to-right sequence begins with heterogeneous architecture sources, passes through a checked dataset, separates durable knowledge from current project state, and forms linked native, structured, and optional learned representations before method choice. A bar across the bottom states that source identity, versions, acquisition conditions, and links remain attached throughout. Native artifacts remain the source of record."}

Within this progression, the split between durable project knowledge and live project state matters most in day-to-day work. A reusable design lesson can outlive the branch that produced it, whereas the hardware, software, workloads, and constraints bound to the active branch change weekly; mixing the two lets an obsolete constraint pass for a current one.

Keeping those records distinct starts with naming the exact information a study needs, and only then identifying the sources that can provide it. Access restrictions shape both steps from the outset, and @sec-architecture-data-access develops their consequences for using and sharing data.

## Why Architecture Data Spans Multiple Tools and Layers

Optimizing against a single data source easily steers a design into a trap: a compiler schedule that minimizes IR instruction count can stall on memory-bank conflicts in cycle simulation, and an RTL block that clears functional simulation can still fail setup timing or routing congestion once mapped to standard cells. No single file or tool captures the whole picture. Specifications state what a system should do, source code and compiler artifacts describe how a computation is organized, simulators and hardware measurements report runtime behavior under particular operating conditions, and physical-design reports establish area, timing, and power costs that a software trace cannot see. Design review notes add context that automated tool logs never record, explaining why an alternative was chosen or ruled out when integration or schedule constraints drove the decision.

Because each source answers only part of the engineering question, collecting more data of one kind cannot make up for a missing link to another. Across the stack, architectural data sources fall into three main families that follow a computation from software down to silicon:

- **Software and compiler artifacts.** Source programs describe the computation, while compiler intermediate representations expose operations, dependencies, and mapping choices such as tiling and scheduling. Binaries pin down the exact executable being evaluated, and execution traces and profiles record its observed runtime behavior. LLVM and Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) provide standard examples of intermediate representations, whose structure and uses are developed in @sec-hardware-representation-formats.
- **Simulation models and execution results.** Simulation models capture selected parts of the hardware and report how a configuration behaves under specific workloads, returning execution cycles, memory transfers, contention, and queue occupancy. Because tools such as gem5, SCALE-Sim, ChampSim, and Ramulator model different structures at different levels of detail, a dataset has to record both what each model represents and which physical effects it leaves out.
- **Implementation artifacts, checks, and measurements.** RTL files and synthesized netlists define hardware implementations, while testbenches, assertions, and verification results check whether those implementations satisfy required behavior. Synthesis and physical-design tools add area, timing, power, and routing measurements under specified cell libraries and clock constraints, and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) prototypes or fabricated silicon provide physical observations with their own test conditions and limits.

Answering a single question in our Lighthouse study requires linking all three families. For a candidate schedule, the compiler's intermediate representation exposes tile dimensions and data reuse, a simulator reports execution cycles, memory transfers, and stalls, and an input-output comparison checks whether the transformed kernel still computes the required result. Joining these sources by candidate and workload identity creates a far more informative sample than storing an isolated latency number: the memory transfers and stalls help explain why a schedule ran fast or slow, while the record's scope makes clear that an isolated kernel simulation still cannot establish whether the complete extended-reality (XR) frame meets its deadline.

Even linked tool runs leave out engineering rationale that only human review can supply. A design review can record an integration constraint, a schedule compromise, or the reason a team rejected an otherwise promising alternative. For a later engineer or automated method to reuse that judgment, the record must preserve the evidence considered, the criteria applied, and the limits of the conclusion, while keeping a rough engineering estimate clearly distinguishable from a tool-checked result (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

Together, these software, simulation, implementation, and review sources define what a complete architectural collection would contain. The next practical question is how much of that linked evidence already exists in accessible datasets, and how much a team must collect for its own study.

## Public Datasets and Their Limits {#sec-public-architecture-datasets}

When a team looks to public repositories to avoid the cost of new simulations and tool flows, it is easy to mistake raw file count for task coverage. A scraped corpus of 100,000 public Verilog modules may look large enough to train a hardware model, yet still contain zero timing-slack reports, workload traces, or verified clock-domain crossing constraints. A public collection does not need to contain everything a study requires, provided its observations actually match the task under evaluation. Judging an existing dataset therefore comes down to three questions: what each sample observes, which properties were checked, and what additional context the study will need. The representative collections in @tbl-public-architecture-data illustrate how public datasets differ across these dimensions.

| **Collection and observation unit** | **Supported task** | **Key missing context** | **Failed or rejected data status** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenRTLSet observes one extracted Verilog module from public Verilog, VHSIC Hardware Description Language (VHDL), or high-level synthesis (HLS) C/C++ [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. | Fine-tuning and evaluating module-level Verilog generation. | Full project state, workload and software conditions, physical measurements, per-module functional checks, and repository-disjoint splits. | Failed VHDL and Vitis HLS conversions are excluded. No corpus of failed artifacts and rejection reasons is released. |
| RTL-Repo observes one target-line completion with surrounding Verilog repository context [@AllamShalan2024RTLRepo]. | Long-context, multi-file Verilog autocompletion evaluated with exact match and edit similarity. | Functional, synthesis, simulation, workload, power, performance, area, and physical-design evidence. Train and test counts do not establish a repository-disjoint split. | No design tool is executed for the observation. Repositories rejected by collection filters are not retained. |
| CircuitNet observes one back-end design run and retained layout under declared synthesis and physical-design settings [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet]. | Cross-stage congestion, design rule check violation, and IR-drop prediction from graph and image-like features. | Front-end software and workload behavior, live project history, and canonical grouping rules. | 12,960 runs attempted; 10,242 layouts retained after excluding failures. Failure causes are not retained. |
| QuArch observes one expert-validated question-answer pair about computer architecture [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArch; @PrakashEtAl2025QuArchReasoning]. | Evaluating architecture knowledge and reasoning, and fine-tuning language models. | Executable design state, workload and software identity, tool returns, physical measurements, and signoff evidence. | In the first release, questions without definitive answers or with narrow scope were removed and not retained. |
: **A dataset supports only the task and context carried by its observations.** Module code, repository context, executed layouts, and architecture questions serve distinct purposes and leave different parts of design decisions unobserved. {#tbl-public-architecture-data tbl-colwidths="[28,20,26,26]"}

Each collection supports a different job because it observes a different slice of design work, and the operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers clarify where each fits. Module corpora such as OpenRTLSet and RTL-Repo observe isolated module text and line completions, which suits Layer 1 point assistance such as drafting or completing a module, yet omits system interfaces, workload behavior, and physical implementation effects such as routing congestion or supply-grid IR drop.[^fn-ir-drop-c04] Layout collections such as CircuitNet instead capture placement and routing outcomes under declared synthesis and physical-design settings, supplying training labels for congestion, design rule violation, or IR-drop predictors that can screen candidates inside a Layer 2 back-end search. Although CircuitNet 2.0 extends this layout family to CPU, GPU, and AI-accelerator designs run through commercial flows at a 14\ nm FinFET node and adds signoff-style timing and power labels [@JiangEtAl2024CircuitNet2], it still stops at the netlist and layout boundary rather than linking back to the compiler schedules or high-level computational graphs that produced the designs. Because a Layer 3 system requires observations linked across that entire span, no public collection examined here suffices on its own, which is why the table places each corpus's capabilities directly beside its missing context and rejected-data policy.

[^fn-ir-drop-c04]: **IR drop**: The voltage decrease that occurs when current ($I$) flows through the resistance ($R$) of the power distribution network. Severe IR drop can cause transistors to switch too slowly, leading to timing violations or outright functional failures.

Even when comparing collection sizes directly, sample counts have to be read in their own units: text corpora count tokens, whereas hardware datasets count modules, layouts, or validated questions. OpenRTLSet contains roughly 131,000 Verilog modules [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet], CircuitNet reports on the order of $10^4$ retained layouts [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet], and QuArch v1.0 contains 2,671 expert-validated question-answer pairs [@PrakashEtAl2025QuArchReasoning]. Because these counts describe fundamentally different observation units, their ratios do not measure how much useful information one collection supplies relative to another.

A narrower observation unit does not imply poor data quality. QuArch evaluates architecture knowledge without describing a live chip project, and CircuitNet provides physical-design observations without recording software behavior. The relevant test is whether the available information supports the intended component, allowing a dataset to serve one part of a design workflow while the team collects missing cross-layer observations separately.

Why public hardware datasets remain so narrow becomes clear when we examine the effort required to construct one. Public source code often needs several filtering and compilation steps before it yields even a synthesizable hardware module.[^fn-hls-synthesizability-c04] The OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection path in @fig-public-code-to-rtl shows how quickly an initially large repository pool narrows through screening and tool conversion.

[^fn-hls-synthesizability-c04]: **High-level synthesis (HLS) synthesizability**: High-level synthesis compiles algorithms expressed in high-level languages (such as C/C++) into RTL. Synthesizable code must stay within a restricted subset of the language. Dynamic memory allocation (for example, `malloc`), unbounded recursion, and operating system calls are generally unsupported, and pointer use is limited, because a circuit needs statically determinable memory sizes, register counts, and scheduling bounds.

```{python}
#| label: fig-public-code-to-rtl
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Building a Verilog corpus from public C/C++ code involves several filters.** The horizontal log-scale bar chart traces repository attrition in the OpenRTLSet C/C++ collection pipeline: approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories narrow to approximately 12,000 after synthesizability screening, and only approximately 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. The resulting 24,000 Verilog modules represent a distinct observation unit from the repositories shown. These counts reflect pipeline-specific tool filters rather than universal hardware synthesizability rates.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Log-scale horizontal bar chart showing three stages from the OpenRTLSet C and C++ collection pipeline. Approximately 103,000 permissively licensed repositories enter the pipeline, 12,000 remain after the authors' synthesizability screen, and 1,000 successfully generate Verilog through Vitis HLS."

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter4-openrtlset-funnel.csv
# (counts transcribed from OpenRTLSet, Section III-A, with per-row source columns)
import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(
    _root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter4-openrtlset-funnel.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    _funnel_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))

# Only the repository-unit stages are plotted; the module count changes units.
_repo_rows = [row for row in _funnel_rows if row["unit"] == "repositories"]
assert len(_repo_rows) == 3
stages = [
    "Collected permissively\nlicensed C/C++ repositories",
    "After authors'\nsynthesizability screen",
    "Successful Vitis HLS\nto Verilog",
]
counts = [int(row["approximate_count"]) for row in _repo_rows]
display_counts = [f"≈{value:,}" for value in counts]
y = [2, 1, 0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8, 2.0))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.38, right=0.92, top=0.9, bottom=0.2)

ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(400, 300_000)

# Bars start at the axis floor and end exactly at each count.
bars = ax.barh(
    y,
    [value - 400 for value in counts],
    left=400,
    height=0.42,
    color=COLORS["workload"],
    edgecolor=COLORS["note_edge"],
    linewidth=0.8,
    zorder=2,
)

for x_value, y_value, label in zip(counts, y, display_counts):
    ax.text(
        x_value * 1.15,
        y_value,
        label,
        ha="left",
        va="center",
        fontsize=6.4,
        fontweight="bold",
        color=COLORS["workload_ink"],
    )

ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(stages, fontsize=6.2)
ax.set_xlabel("approximate repositories remaining (log scale)", fontsize=6.2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0, pad=5)
ax.grid(axis="x", color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.6, zorder=1)

for spine in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
```

The collection starts from permissively licensed repositories, screens them for synthesizability with a regular-expression checker, and then attempts conversion with Vitis HLS [@WangEtAl2025OpenRTLSet]. Roughly 103,000 repositories narrow to approximately 1,000 that generate Verilog, largely because ordinary C/C++ relies on constructs that high-level synthesis cannot map to a circuit. That steep attrition measures how hard it is to extract hardware from unannotated software rather than how much digital design exists, and even the surviving repositories yield only generated Verilog modules without matching physical implementations or workload measurements. Source code to seed a corpus may be abundant, but obtaining the linked physical observations needed to answer an architectural question still demands substantial tool execution.

Because open repositories provide abundant source text but very few executed implementations, a foundation model pretrained on public corpora can learn syntax, circuit idioms, and documented design rules,[^fn-foundation-model-c04] yet still lack the evidence needed to apply those rules under project conditions. Assessing clock-domain crossings for metastability risk,[^fn-metastability-c04] managing power-grid voltage drops, and preventing combinational loops all require running verification and timing checks on the proposed design itself. That gap between syntax and verified implementation connects corpus quality directly to the evaluation bottleneck in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales: generating a plausible artifact and qualifying it consume very different resources.

[^fn-metastability-c04]: **Metastability**: A transient state in which a storage element has not resolved to a valid logic level within the expected time. A setup or hold violation, including one caused by an asynchronous input, can produce it. Synchronizers reduce the probability that unresolved behavior reaches downstream logic; they do not eliminate the possibility of metastability.

[^fn-foundation-model-c04]: **Foundation model**: A model pretrained on broad data at scale and then adapted to many downstream tasks rather than trained for a single one [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels]. The term comes from machine learning, and this chapter treats such a model as one optional component inside a design system rather than as the design system itself.

Internal project archives can fill some of these gaps for in-house teams, subject to the access restrictions discussed in @sec-architecture-data-access. ChipNeMo, for example, adapts a language model using proprietary chip-design material for engineering assistance, electronic design automation (EDA) script generation, and bug summarization [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. Using internal material improves domain performance without making that material publicly reproducible, so an evaluation still has to state which evidence an independent reviewer can inspect.

For our Lighthouse mapping study, the gap left by existing collections is concrete. Neither architecture question-answer pairs nor physical-layout observations supply the schedule-latency pairs needed to compare software schedules on the candidate NPU. Those observations have to be collected or adapted from a compatible source, connecting the source kernels, candidate schedules, hardware target, correctness checks, and execution results before the dataset can support a comparison.

Public availability therefore answers only the first part of the data question. Once an engineering team knows what existing collections contribute, it can identify the missing observations and decide how to collect them at a cost and coverage that fit the study.

## Collecting Architectural Data

Launching a data-collection sweep without an explicit plan can burn weeks of cluster compute and tool licenses while leaving the study's central question unanswered: a team can run thousands of cycle simulations on a single convenient input shape, or synthesize netlists at one nominal corner, only to discover that the decisive memory-traffic or timing bottleneck was never exercised. Even in a software-focused experiment like the Lighthouse mapping study, testing a schedule change requires new compilation, numerical verification, and simulator execution. Planning that collection therefore requires balancing three coupled choices: the tool path used to evaluate a candidate, the compute and engineering resources required per sample, and the workloads or operating conditions covered.

### Choosing Tools That Can See the Bottleneck

Choosing a fast evaluation tool that is blind to bus arbitration or layout parasitics can certify a candidate right across a contention or timing cliff, because the physical effect that breaks the design never enters the model. Which tool path a study needs depends on the question it asks: in the Lighthouse mapping study, comparing compiler schedules requires execution results that capture computation and data movement, whereas estimating the physical cost of the accelerator itself requires synthesis and layout tools. Because each tool answers one question well while leaving others unresolved, the alternatives in @tbl-observation-source-limits trade observation scope and modeling assumptions against acquisition cost.

| **Source** | **Useful for** | **Important limit to represent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical model | Fast sensitivity studies and early bounds. | Simplifying equations, calibration range, and omitted interactions. |
| SystemC / transaction-level modeling (TLM) 2.0 virtual platform | Rapid transaction-level memory and interconnect throughput exploration and early software bring-up. | Pin-level clock timing, detailed gate delays, layout parasitics, and unmodeled contention. |
| Trace-driven simulator (ChampSim, Ramulator 2) | Repeatable study of memory access streams, cache hierarchies, and DRAM bus scheduling under captured workloads. | No timing feedback absent from the trace, and no unmodeled bus states. |
| Cycle-level simulator (gem5, SCALE-Sim) | Detailed modeled microarchitectural behavior across CPU cores, NPU accelerators, and interconnects. | Simulator abstractions, unsupported states, calibration, and execution cost. |
| Gate-level netlist simulation | Pin-level logic verification, cell delay evaluation, and X-propagation (the rippling of unknown or uninitialized states through logic gates) under synthesized netlists. | Testbench coverage, runtime overhead, timing abstractions, and unmodeled layout parasitics. |
| RTL simulation (Verilator, VCS) | Logic, interface, and microarchitectural behavior over the exercised testbench. | Stimulus identity, functional coverage, simulator version, and unmodeled physical delays. |
| Formal analysis (SystemVerilog Assertions / bounded model checking) | Proof, counterexample, bounded-only, or inconclusive status for a stated property and assumptions. | Stated property, assumptions, abstraction, proof method, bound, vacuity checks, and status. |
| Synthesis and STA / power analysis (Yosys, Design Compiler, OpenSTA) | Logic transformation, technology mapping, and static timing analysis (STA), area, or power estimates within the flow. | Libraries, modes, corners, constraints, tool versions, and physical approximations. |
| Place-and-route and physical verification (OpenROAD, Innovus) | Placement, routing, extraction, timing, power integrity, and design rule checking (DRC) results for the implemented database. | Floorplan state, signoff models, modes, corners, waivers, tool versions, and manufacturing models. |
| FPGA or emulation platform | High-throughput functional or timing-model execution after mapping. | Mapping differences, compile cost, debug visibility, and non-transferable application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) power or timing. |
| Fabricated silicon | Behavior of a physical implementation under measured conditions. | Limited design variants, observability, stepping, test conditions, and inability to answer counterfactual questions. |
: **Every observation source has a useful scope and a blind spot.** Recording both ensures appropriate tool selection and qualification in downstream chapters. {#tbl-observation-source-limits tbl-colwidths="[22,36,42]"}

As the table shows, a clean result from one tool cannot substitute for an unmodeled check in another: a timing-closure report on a gate-level netlist says nothing about routed power-grid droop, and a transaction-level throughput estimate does not bound cycle-accurate tail latency when flits contend for the same link. Attaching these modeling limits to each observation lets a downstream method distinguish a fast early proxy from a measurement of the target property.

Even within a single tool, hardware measurements depend on the operating conditions under which they were obtained. In an illustrative multiplier example, suppose static timing analysis reports a 1.1\ ns cycle time at an assumed typical corner (0.85\ V, $25^\circ\text{C}$). Evaluating that same design at a second assumed corner (0.72\ V, $125^\circ\text{C}$) or under a different clock-tree skew target may change whether the implementation closes timing.[^fn-timing-closure-c04] (These values illustrate the context a record must retain; they are not measurements of a particular multiplier or foundry process, and they do not determine the size of a timing violation.) A timing or power label is therefore incomplete without the implementation and analysis conditions that produced it.

[^fn-timing-closure-c04]: **Timing closure and operating corners**: Timing closure establishes that the analyzed paths meet their specified timing requirements, including setup and hold, under the selected models and constraints. Process, voltage, and temperature affect delays; the limiting corner can differ by path and check. Passing the required corners supports those timing claims, not a guarantee against every silicon failure.

To keep these dependencies explicit, we can describe each evaluated candidate by the context-bound tuple $\mathcal{O} = \langle s_{\text{design}}, w_{\text{workload}}, \tau_{\text{tool}}, \kappa_{\text{corner}}, y_{\text{metrics}} \rangle$. Here $s_{\text{design}}$ denotes the microarchitectural and RTL configuration together with the candidate's software choices; $w_{\text{workload}}$ identifies the application inputs, execution phase, and matching binary; $\tau_{\text{tool}}$ identifies the compiler and evaluation toolchain; $\kappa_{\text{corner}}$ specifies the process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions where applicable; and $y_{\text{metrics}}$ contains the returned measurements. Just as a latency number in the mapping study is incomplete without its schedule and hardware target, a power estimate requires the implementation and switching-activity assumptions that produced it, and the tuple records these dependencies without implying that every tool supplies every field.

### The Compute and License Cost of Collecting Samples

In the Lighthouse mapping study, sample acquisition begins well before timed execution: each candidate schedule must compile for the target, pass output correctness checks, and load into the evaluation environment before a simulator or hardware run can return latency and diagnostic counters. While preparing the compiler backend or calibrating the accelerator model is a shared upfront investment, compilation, testing, execution, and diagnosis accumulate per candidate and multiply across repeated runs and workload shapes, so a dataset budget that counts only the final timing call misses much of the work required to produce a usable label.

Once a candidate clears compilation and correctness checks, timed simulation often dominates the per-sample cost. We can quantify the effect of execution coverage independently of a particular Lighthouse candidate by considering an illustrative 1\ GHz target, a 1\ s measured interval, 0.2\ s of warmup, a simulator rate of 100,000 target cycles per wall-clock second, three repetitions, and four workloads.

```{python}
#| echo: false

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

# Source data: data/datasets/chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
with open(
    _root / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter4-simulation-time-explosion.csv",
    encoding="utf-8",
) as fh:
    # datasets carry '#' provenance headers; skip them
    _simulation_cost_rows = list(csv.DictReader(l for l in fh if not l.startswith("#")))

_one_second_row = next(
    row
    for row in _simulation_cost_rows
    if row["target_workload_duration"] == "1 s"
)
measurement_cycles = int(_one_second_row["target_cycles_at_1ghz"])
warmup_cycles = measurement_cycles // 5
simulator_rate = 100_000
repetitions = 3
workloads = 4
single_measurement_hours = measurement_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
total_target_cycles = (
    (warmup_cycles + measurement_cycles) * repetitions * workloads
)
total_serial_hours = total_target_cycles / simulator_rate / 3_600
assert _one_second_row["wall_time_at_100kcycle_s"] == "2.8 h"
assert round(total_target_cycles / 1e9, 1) == 14.4
assert round(total_serial_hours) == 40
```

During a single measured interval of 1\ s, a 1\ GHz target executes one billion cycles ($10^9$). At an assumed simulator rate of 100,000 target cycles per wall-clock second, simulating that single second takes roughly 2.8\ hours. Serial execution cost $T_{\text{serial}}$ combines target warmup cycles $C_{\text{warmup}}$, target measurement cycles $C_{\text{measure}}$, repetition count $R$, workload count $W$, and simulator throughput $v_{\text{sim}}$:

$$
T_{\text{serial}} =
\frac{(C_{\text{warmup}} + C_{\text{measure}}) \times R \times W}
{v_{\text{sim}}}.
$${#eq-serial-execution-cost}

If we evaluate four workloads across three repetitions under the assumptions in @eq-serial-execution-cost, the study executes 14.4 billion target cycles and consumes forty serial simulator hours.[^fn-simulation-warmup-c04]

[^fn-simulation-warmup-c04]: **Simulation warmup**: Architectural simulators begin execution with uninitialized (cold) state in caches, branch target buffers, translation lookaside buffers (TLBs), and prefetchers. Simulating an initial interval ($C_{\text{warmup}}$) without gathering statistics warms up internal microarchitectural structures to realistic steady-state hit rates before the actual measurement window begins.

Those forty hours represent accumulated simulator runtime for one candidate configuration. Running jobs in parallel across a cluster can shorten wall-clock collection time when compute nodes and licenses permit, but it does not reduce total machine time, and shared setup, compilation, correctness checks, queueing, and failure diagnosis add further cost beyond the execution estimate.

Replacing direct simulation with a fast surrogate does not eliminate that upfront acquisition budget either. Even if a surrogate evaluates a candidate in an illustrative two milliseconds, it still requires reference tool runs for training and calibration, whose collection can consume days or weeks of cluster compute. In BOOM-Explorer, for example, the authors built an offline dataset of 994 sampled microarchitectural configurations, and running the very-large-scale integration (VLSI) flow for each design took from about six to more than fourteen hours [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. At those per-sample costs, sweeping millions of variations requires a staged acquisition strategy rather than exhaustive evaluation.

Because every observation carries a real compute and engineering price, recording resource consumption alongside the measurements helps the team budget further collection. Execution time, memory footprint, license demand, and human debugging effort determine which evaluation paths remain practical at different scales, while the run's operating conditions and check status establish what that expenditure actually proved. Together, these details let a later user judge both whether an observation is trustworthy and what obtaining comparable samples would cost (@tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels).

| **Dataset simplification** | **Architecture sample** | **Consequence for later use** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cheap acquisition** | Results require scarce licenses, long tool runs, fabrication, setup, diagnosis, and expert review. | Records must capture resources and human work required to obtain the result. |
| **Fixed ground-truth label** | Tools return results for named properties at stated fidelities under recorded conditions. | Properties, checks, fidelities, and conditions must be preserved for interpretation. |
| **Independent, interchangeable rows** | Results frequently share ancestors, generated artifacts, traces, images, seeds, or earlier decisions. | Lineage must be preserved to avoid counting dependent results as independent support. |
| **Missing data without structure** | Failed, timed-out, and rejected runs are selectively lost; some violations reveal only threshold crossings. | Run status, failure reasons, and censored bounds must be retained rather than learning only from survivors. |
| **Matching attributes imply comparability** | Two rows support comparison only when candidate identities, permitted differences, workloads, and tool paths match. | Results with uncontrolled differences must be treated as advisory context rather than matched comparisons. |
: **Architecture samples are costly, conditioned results.** Their meaning and comparability depend on lineage, property checks, acquisition status, and matched study conditions. {#tbl-architecture-observations-not-labels tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

### Workload Coverage and Representative Sampling

Once the price of a single evaluation is clear, the next question is which workload executions deserve that budget. Static hardware descriptions show what a system can execute, but running workloads determine which datapaths become active, which queues saturate, and which memory banks stall. Because full applications run for billions of cycles, a short trace slice is useful only if it captures the runtime behavior that governs the architectural decision.

In our Lighthouse XR workload, what a sample must include depends on the system boundary under test. An isolated kernel measurement needs its input tensor shape, data type, and schedule, whereas a full-frame measurement also needs the surrounding pipeline stages and their execution overlap. Because the subsystem's 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope applies to all work inside that boundary, an isolated kernel that runs fast on its own may still wait for upstream inputs or contend with rendering when integrated. The dataset must therefore distinguish isolated-kernel observations from frame-level observations instead of treating both as interchangeable labels for the same target.

Even at the right boundary, workload coverage has to match the metric being evaluated. A trace collection chosen to estimate average throughput can miss brief memory-bus stalls that decide whether a perception frame meets its real-time deadline. Before selecting representative intervals, an evaluation plan has to identify which workload behaviors could flip the architectural conclusion.

System performance, power dissipation, and thermal behavior are joint outcomes $y = f(x, w)$ of the hardware configuration $x \in \mathcal{X}$ and the dynamic workload feature vector $w \in \mathcal{W}$. Changing the application software or moving to a different execution phase can shift a hardware candidate from compute-bound to memory-bound. To capture these runtime shifts without paying for full-trace simulation, architects compress execution traces into compact feature representations.

SimPoint, for example, builds basic block vectors ($w_{\text{BBV}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$) by counting how often each static basic block executes during fixed instruction intervals (such as $10^7$ or $10^8$ instructions), weighting those counts by static block length, and normalizing across the interval [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint].[^fn-simpoint-c04] Projecting those interval vectors into a lower-dimensional space (for example, via random projection) and clustering them with $k$-means identifies recurring program phases, allowing a small set of weighted simulation intervals (SimPoints) to estimate full-trace behavior.

[^fn-simpoint-c04]: **SimPoint**: A methodology that clusters program-execution intervals and selects representatives for weighted simulation estimates. It can reduce simulation cost; accuracy depends on the selected intervals, target metrics, and evaluation conditions.

Clustering program phases reduces simulation cost, but it does not automatically supply an error bound for a new design; the architect still has to verify how accurately the selected intervals estimate the target metrics. When a study requires explicit statistical confidence intervals over sampled execution slices, systematic sampling methods such as SMARTS compute those bounds directly under their sampling assumptions [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS].

For modern accelerator and transformer workloads, compact workload descriptors extend beyond basic block counts to capture key-value (KV) cache footprints and decoding burst lengths. Together with basic block vectors and memory-stride histograms, these phase embeddings can condition a learned performance predictor on runtime workload behavior and represent the workload portion of a design loop's state, developed in @sec-hardware-representation-formats.

Whether a team can reuse captured traces or phase descriptors across candidates depends on whether the compiler output changes. In the Lighthouse mapping study, a new loop tiling or scheduling choice alters the memory-access stream itself, so replaying an old schedule's trace would not evaluate the new schedule; the workload inputs and comparison window stay matched, but each candidate must generate its own trace. Basic block vectors likewise stay bound to the compiled binary, collection policy, frame identifiers, and execution parameters that produced them. That dependency separates a software-changing mapping study from a hardware cache study that holds the compiled software image fixed across candidates.

### Recording Simulator Flags, Tool Versions, and Operating Corners

If a simulator flag, compiler version, or static random-access memory (SRAM) process corner drifts silently between Tuesday's baseline run and Friday's candidate run, the dataset will attribute that environmental shift to the hardware change. Preventing such false attributions requires binding the evaluation path, acquisition cost, and workload coverage together in every recorded sample. In the Lighthouse cache comparison introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology, holding the software fixed while varying cache capacity means capturing both the hardware design state $s_{\text{design}}$ (repository commit hashes, macro parameters, and SRAM compiler configurations) and the environmental state (workload dataset, software image version, and representative instruction window).

The remaining fields of the observation tuple $\mathcal{O}$ specify what an execution record must capture to make the evaluation reproducible: $\tau_{\text{tool}}$ pins the simulator versions, flags, and container digest; $\kappa_{\text{corner}}$ names the process corner, voltage rail, and temperature; and $y_{\text{metrics}}$ pairs reported quantities (such as 99th-percentile frame time, subsystem power, macro area, and access latency) directly with their measurement sources and execution costs.

Together, these fields serve as comparison keys linking the study revision, design revision, candidate configuration, workload snapshot, software image, toolchain manifest, and physical operating conditions. Matched rows in a dataset support a clean comparison only when they agree on the fixed conditions and trace design differences solely to the permitted capacity change. When a run times out or fails to route, the record retains all of these context identities alongside any qualified partial results, marks unmeasured metrics as unavailable, and logs the failure class rather than dropping the run or substituting an artificial penalty score.

## Constructing Architecture Datasets

Provenance records keep a single observation intact, but building an architectural dataset requires deciding which observations belong together and which parts of the design space they should cover. Because the acquisition costs derived earlier limit how many runs a team can afford, simply collecting convenient simulation logs and Verilog files often leaves the cases that distinguish competing designs untested.

In our Lighthouse mapping study, for example, the collection plan must cover the operator shapes and schedules that could flip which candidate wins. If a team evaluates dozens of tile sizes on a single convenient matrix shape, the rest of the perception workload remains unrepresented. A useful initial dataset instead spans distinct reuse patterns and working-set sizes, including shapes that push against the target's local memory limits, while reserving evaluation budget to check whether an apparent kernel speedup survives integration into the full frame workload.

Whether a dataset is adequate therefore depends on the specific comparison it has to resolve. More repetitions characterize run-to-run variation, new input shapes close a workload coverage gap, and another hardware target tests cross-platform transfer; all three compete for the same acquisition budget and cannot substitute for one another. In the smaller cache study, the dataset is adequate only if matched runs clearly separate the 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB candidates from the 2\ MiB baseline while checking each candidate against the SRAM area and power limits. Whenever the available observations leave a comparison undecided, the next sample should target the specific uncertainty blocking that decision.

### Multi-Fidelity Sampling

Because cycle-accurate simulation and physical layout are too slow to run on every candidate while analytical formulas are too coarse to certify a winner, teams often combine cheap and expensive evaluations in the same dataset. Done carelessly, pooling rough roofline bounds and cycle-accurate measurements into a single unlabeled latency column teaches a predictor to treat approximation error as hardware behavior. *Multi-fidelity sampling* stretches a fixed acquisition budget safely by pairing inexpensive estimates with costly simulations or implementation runs, provided the sources estimate the same output or have an explicit relationship between their outputs [@PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity] and each row records which tool produced it. Within that budget, active learning can allocate further observations by selecting examples expected to improve a model or reduce uncertainty [@Settles2009ActiveLearning], although its usefulness depends on whether those selections repay their acquisition cost.

In the mapping study, inexpensive analytical estimates can screen many candidate schedules while cycle-level evaluations examine selected candidates near constraint boundaries or decision crossovers, leaving unvisited regions unsupported. When an adaptive selection policy picks those follow-up samples from earlier results, the dataset must also record its selection rules, candidate pools, and available observations; otherwise, a later evaluation cannot tell whether its test cases already steered the sampling loop [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout].

### Cleaning Logs and Preventing Train-Test Leakage

Even carefully collected tool runs can be ruined during dataset assembly if a regular-expression log parser silently turns a negative timing slack or missing report into `0.0`, or if a random train-test split scatters variants from the same Chisel or SystemVerilog generator template across both partitions. Curation is what prevents those pipeline bugs from masquerading as clean training data. In the mapping dataset, each row identifies a kernel, input shape, schedule, and hardware target, and links to its compiled artifact, correctness result, repeated timings, and diagnostic counters, with consistent units, grouped repetitions, and missing results kept distinct from measured zeros. The source kernel and transformation history also supply the grouping keys needed for evaluation splits, because holding out new schedules for a familiar kernel tests a different capability from holding out an operator family that never appeared in training.

Those grouping keys matter because training examples in a hardware table are rarely independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.). Multiple rows often share a design ancestor, generated artifact, workload trace, or software image, and repeated evaluations of a single schedule measure run-to-run variation rather than independent programs. When the dataset records those lineage links explicitly, an evaluation split can test the intended form of transfer and prevent a high row count from disguising a narrow set of underlying designs.

Protected evaluation splits must therefore follow the transfer claim (design family, workload, software revision, or time period) rather than random row partitioning [@KapoorNarayanan2023Leakage]. Parameterized hardware description language (HDL) generators make this requirement especially strict: because every configuration elaborates the same underlying subgraphs, separating table rows without separating their generating templates only tests whether a model recognizes a familiar template rather than whether it generalizes to a new design family.

Pipeline construction must also guard against *data contamination*, because exposure to public hardware benchmarks during training can inflate evaluation scores through memorization rather than genuine generalization to new designs [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated; @Balloccu2024Leakage]. Because private testbenches, repository-disjoint splits, and behavior-preserving transformations of test artifacts address different exposure risks, no single measure is mandatory or sufficient for every study; instead, a dataset record should state which exposure paths were examined, what each measure protects, and whether any transformed tasks still test the claimed capability.

Synthetic training examples require similar qualification matched to their intended use, since treating unverified generator outputs as measured observations can mislead downstream learning [@VanBreugelEtAl2023SyntheticData]. Methods such as CraftRTL use synthetic Verilog examples to repair model errors [@LiuEtAl2024CraftRTL], yet passing syntax checks does not establish functional behavior, and passing functional tests says nothing about timing or power. A dataset can retain examples at any of these stages if it records the generator identity, intended task, and completed checks, while reserving physical evaluation for labels that make a physical claim.

Finally, the extraction scripts that assemble tool outputs into table columns require the same scrutiny as the splits. The term *data cascades* describes how upstream data problems produce delayed errors in downstream work [@SambasivanEtAl2021DataCascades]. In architecture studies, a parser that drops a minus sign on timing slack or classifies license exhaustion as a design failure turns raw tool returns into mislabeled training examples, introducing label noise that must be caught and corrected before it distorts what a model learns [@NorthcuttJiangChuang2021ConfidentLearning]. An unrecorded compiler flag or source transformation can similarly alter a comparison's meaning without leaving a trace in the feature columns. When the pipeline links every computed attribute back to its raw tool returns and extraction scripts, a reviewer can detect such bugs and determine which conclusions they affect.

### Preserving Failed and Censored Execution Runs

Discarding failed tool runs or collapsing every non-passing return into a single `fail` bit corrupts a dataset in two ways: dropping unroutable or timing-violating layouts blinds a surrogate predictor to the physical feasibility boundary, while logging a dropped FlexLM license connection as a design failure teaches an optimizer to avoid a valid region of the search space. To keep those cases distinct, a dataset pipeline must record what an evaluation attempt actually established across five outcome classes:

- *Infrastructure faults* (such as floating-license exhaustion or network interruption) identify problems with the execution environment rather than an infeasible design, although a simulator crash still requires diagnosis before a team assigns it to this category and chooses a repair or retry policy.
- *Syntax and typing defects* (such as undeclared wires or bitwidth mismatches) identify errors in a proposed artifact, where repair may require changing the artifact, its generator, or the transformation that produced it.
- *Constraint violations* (such as negative setup slack, unroutability, or exceeded power delivery network (PDN) IR-drop limits) identify a failed requirement under the recorded implementation and tool conditions. They constrain reuse under those conditions without proving that every implementation of the architecture must fail.
- *Formal verification results* distinguish proofs, counterexamples, bounded results, and inconclusive returns, where each retains its property, assumptions, and proof scope because a bounded check cannot establish behavior beyond its horizon.
- *Resource-limit stops* retain the elapsed budget, partial results, and unresolved property when a timeout could reflect candidate complexity, tool behavior, or infrastructure rather than identifying a single cause on its own.

In a compiler-schedule search, a fast schedule that computes the wrong answer is not a valid speedup, whereas an unexplained compiler crash does not prove that the schedule is infeasible on the target hardware. Retaining the inputs, raw tool returns, and failure classification together lets diagnostic scripts and training pipelines separate environment faults from broken candidates.

For physical design runs, retaining constraint violations also prevents survivorship bias during model training. Because a measured timing or routing violation supplies concrete signal right at the feasibility boundary, training a surrogate exclusively on clean signoff runs omits outcomes that depend directly on the quantities being predicted, which biases statistical inference [@Rubin1976InferenceMissingData]. Keeping unsuccessful attempts alongside passing measurements preserves that boundary information without confusing failed candidates with working ones.

A censored observation establishes a bound on a named quantity rather than its exact value.[^fn-censored-c04] A timed-out simulation might establish $y \ge y_{\text{limit}}$ for dynamic execution latency, for example, whereas an EDA tool timeout supplies no such bound on circuit path delay because an incomplete place-and-route run lacks extracted layout parasitics, leaving physical interconnect delays unbounded. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization examines how predictive and search methods incorporate these qualified labels and bounds.

[^fn-censored-c04]: **Censored observation**: The result establishes only that a value lies above or below a threshold rather than reporting the value itself [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. A failed target-frequency test is left-censored because it establishes that maximum sustainable frequency lies below the target.

A versioned execution history separates attempt status, candidate outcome, and project updates so that data-cleaning routines do not conflate tool failures with design evidence (@fig-execution-history). With all three recorded separately, a later reader or search method can distinguish a completed check that rejected a candidate from an aborted attempt that left it unresolved.

![**Execution history tracking preserves status, outcome, and cost attributes.** Decoupling tool execution completion from candidate qualification outcomes and project commits prevents automated flows from discarding useful negative evidence. Preserving attempt attributes and diagnostic reasons allows later methods to determine whether an earlier failure reflects an intrinsic architectural barrier or an obsolete tool configuration. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-execution-history){#fig-execution-history width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram of a versioned execution history with separate attempt status, candidate outcome, and project update attributes. One completed attempt advances a candidate and creates a new project version. A second completed attempt leaves the candidate rejected or unresolved and makes no project update. A third attempt completes on stale inputs, which yields no usable candidate outcome for the current comparison and leaves project state unchanged."}

The stale-input path is the case a single pass/fail bit cannot represent: the tool exits cleanly and the run looks successful, but its inputs no longer match the active baseline, yielding no usable outcome for the current comparison. That separation between attempt status and candidate outcome is what stops an automated search from treating a stale success as a valid baseline, or mistaking a timeout for an architectural refutation.

In our mapping study, for instance, an old schedule's timing result can remain useful training material for a broad cost model even after a new compiler release disqualifies it as a matched baseline comparison. Because its value depends on how later work intends to use it and which conditions changed, an explicit execution history preserves the run for training without presenting it as a current measurement.

More generally, what a failed evaluation can teach depends on why it failed (@tbl-negative-traces). When the dataset pairs root-cause diagnostics with the failure label, search algorithms can separate environment glitches from design violations under the tested conditions, while recognizing that neither the label nor the diagnosis makes a boundary permanent once the design or its operating conditions change.

| **Failed run or rejected alternative** | **Preserved information** | **How later work should use it** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synthesis or timing violation** | Candidate, constraints, process assumptions, and failing paths. | Reconsider the candidate only after checking whether relevant conditions still apply. |
| **Unroutable or power failure** | Netlist, placement conditions, density, congestion, or IR-drop result. | Identify the affected region without treating the failure as characteristic of all similar designs. |
| **Proxy improvement overturned** | Cheap estimate, later observation, and precise divergence conditions. | Reassess the proxy's useful scope before attempting reuse. |
| **Tool failure or crash** | Command, inputs, environment identity, logs, and failure classification. | Diagnose the cause; repair infrastructure when established as the cause. Otherwise retain unresolved status until evidence supports classification. |
| **Coverage gap** | Missing workload, input, scenario, or architecture class. | Mark the strict boundary of the result rather than filling it with assumptions. |
| **Reviewer rejection** | Candidate, stated reason, risk, schedule, integration concern, and owner. | Preserve rationale and revisit only when relevant conditions fundamentally change. |
| **Waiver or exception** | Violated rule, justification, scope, owner, and expiration condition. | Prevent repeated work while keeping the granted exception visible. |
: **Rejected work remains useful when conditions are systematically recorded.** Explicit failure conditions allow subsequent architects to determine whether historical boundaries still apply. {#tbl-negative-traces tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

These diagnostic records also point to what the next experiment should test. In the mapping study, a schedule whose buffers exceed local-memory capacity directly motivates trying a smaller tile or a different staging pattern; the diagnosed failure gives the next run a clear hypothesis while leaving open which revision will succeed.

## Turning Raw Tool Runs into Reusable Design Knowledge

While curated observations establish what happened under particular test conditions, turning those records into durable architectural knowledge requires explaining *why* the result occurred well enough to guide another decision. Suppose evaluations in our Lighthouse mapping study found that one schedule reduced both off-chip transfers and execution time on matched inputs, suggesting that its tiling kept intermediate data in local memory for reuse. Because the timing result alone does not establish that mechanism, an architect needs the transfer counts, stall behavior, and generated schedule to test that explanation against alternatives such as a change in parallelism or instruction overhead (an illustrative interpretation rather than a reported Lighthouse result).

Once checked, the reusable lesson states when that schedule helps: it accelerates shapes whose working sets fit in the available local memory, whereas larger shapes require additional off-chip transfers and lose the benefit. Contrasting those passing and spilling cases turns an isolated ranking into a conditional explanation, provided the supporting runs, counterexamples, and remaining uncertainty stay linked to it. Without those links, a later method may reuse the winning tile size after the workload or memory organization has changed, even though the physical reason it worked no longer applies.

That boundary separates three kinds of project records: *raw data* captures source observations, *durable knowledge* encompasses reusable design principles, checked specifications, and architectural explanations, and *live project state* identifies the hardware, software, workload, and constraints governing current work. An explanation can remain useful long after the specific candidate that produced it has changed, but applying it to new work requires checking whether current conditions still match. A learned model may suggest a familiar scheduling pattern from its training corpus, while the active compiler artifacts and workload description establish whether that pattern actually applies to the candidate under test. The information sources in @tbl-knowledge-objects contribute distinct parts of this judgment.

| **Information source** | **What it contributes** | **What to check before reuse** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Trained-model weights** | Learned statistical regularities and general concepts. | Use as prior knowledge; consult project sources for the current design and constraints. |
| **Retrieved material** | Manuals, papers, examples, and project documents. | Check the underlying source and whether its version applies to the intended use. |
| **In-context working set** | Instructions, selected sources, current state, and operational examples. | Check which sources were supplied. Text in a model's context does not itself update the design. |
| **Defined comparison** | Question, comparator, scope, permitted changes, constraints, budget, and stop rules. | Confirm that the comparison still uses the intended baseline and permits the proposed change. |
| **Design and software artifacts** | Configuration, generated hardware, software images, manifests, and constraints. | Identify the hardware and software versions being evaluated, and distinguish checks already completed from those still required. |
| **Workload data** | Traces, profiles, observed population, phase definitions, and sampling policy. | Check whether the captured inputs and phases cover the behavior relevant to the new question. |
| **Project history** | Prior candidates, tool runs, failures, decisions, and rationale linked to conditions. | Check whether the conditions supporting an earlier conclusion still apply. |
: **Reusing knowledge requires checking the information that makes it applicable.** Models, documents, artifacts, and observations contribute different parts of that judgment; none substitutes for all the others. {#tbl-knowledge-objects tbl-colwidths="[20,34,46]"}

These sources age at different rates and become outdated for different reasons. A general scheduling principle may remain valid while the interface specification needed to apply it has changed, and allowing an obsolete constraint into an active evaluation loop can split a proposal from the checks meant to verify it.[^fn-split-brain-c04] When a generator pulls a bus width or clock frequency from outdated documentation while targeting the current implementation, its proposal can be syntactically clean and internally consistent while violating the parameters governing the rest of the system (@fig-split-brain-causality).

[^fn-split-brain-c04]: **Stale constraint optimization**: A proposal is generated or evaluated against an outdated requirement. It may pass checks using that same stale requirement while violating the current design's interface, timing, or functional obligations.

![**Outdated specifications can produce internally consistent designs that conflict with the current system.** If a generator or retrieval model queries frozen reference collateral while active project state advances to revised interfaces, candidate proposals can satisfy local syntax while violating global system constraints. Verifying artifact freshness and source identities before tool dispatch prevents stale proposals from consuming downstream simulation and synthesis budgets. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-split-brain-causality){#fig-split-brain-causality width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram in which a stale reference state and a current project state lead to an incompatible proposal. Version and freshness checks expose the mismatch before the proposal reaches a costly tool flow."}

A stale interface assumption easily survives syntax parsing and isolated module synthesis because neither check inspects the system-level boundary, so the mismatch usually surfaces during integration or later, when repair is most expensive. Freshness and input-identity checks before tool dispatch expose that version divergence before the proposal consumes simulation and synthesis budget, though confirming full interface compatibility still requires functional checks against the active design.

Updates to live project state carry their own compute, storage, license, and review costs. Whenever a compiler release, a new workload capture, or a revised bus specification makes part of the recorded knowledge inapplicable, the team needs a way to detect what went stale and decide which records to refresh. A smaller set of verified, up-to-date sources is therefore more useful to an active design loop than a broad archive whose applicability is unclear.

Once observations are organized and their explanations are tied to live project conditions, the next decision is how to represent that information for computation. An explanation that guides a human architect does not automatically supply the numerical features a predictor consumes or the structural primitives a generator can modify.

## Machine-Usable Hardware Representations {#sec-hardware-representation-formats}

Feeding every column of a curated dataset into a model can easily leak post-execution measurements into a pre-execution predictor: if a latency surrogate is trained with dynamic memory-transfer counts and simulator stall cycles among its input features, it will look accurate on held-out table rows yet be unusable at screening time before the simulator has run. Because the mapping dataset records more context than any single component can legally read when it acts, each representation must expose only the features available at that step of the workflow. A pre-execution latency predictor can take the operator shape, data type, loop organization, tile sizes, and target-memory parameters as inputs while using measured latency as its training target, leaving dynamic transfer counts and stall cycles for post-run diagnosis unless a separate upstream model estimates them first. AutoTVM illustrates how program structure supports this pre-execution role by feeding its cost models features extracted from low-level loop programs or learned representations of their syntax trees [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM].

A generator, by contrast, needs a representation it can legally modify. A vector of tile sizes describes alternatives within a fixed schedule template, but proposing a different ordering or fusion of operations requires access to data dependencies and supported transformations so that the resulting schedule maps cleanly to compiler inputs and preserves numerical behavior. In our Lighthouse study, the same data-design question asks what representations a prospective accelerator target requires, without assuming that a trained cost model or compiler backend is already in place.

### Structure Beyond Token Sequences

Hardware description languages illustrate the consequences of this representation choice for circuits. SystemVerilog and VHDL encode concurrent hardware in linear text, yet token order does not directly expose circuit connectivity or timing relationships: two signals that sit far apart in a source file may share the same critical path. A model consuming RTL as a flat token sequence must reconstruct those relationships from identifiers, whereas a circuit graph exposes connectivity directly and links to cell libraries and constraint files for the electrical context absent from the RTL. Even so, neither representation alone establishes capacitive fanout loading, clock-domain crossing (CDC) safety, or setup-hold[^fn-setup-hold-c04] timing across physical operating corners.

[^fn-setup-hold-c04]: **Setup and hold times**: Timing requirements for a register's data input around the sampling clock edge. Setup time specifies how long the data must be stable before the edge; hold time specifies how long it must remain stable afterward, under the characterized conditions. A violation can cause metastability or incorrect capture.

Protocol interfaces show why syntax alone is insufficient at the behavioral level as well, since a model can generate a plausible token sequence that wires the wrong signals, violates an interconnect handshake, drops a reset condition, or references a stale module hierarchy. If a generated Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) Stream bridge must throttle its upstream sender when its first-in, first-out (FIFO) buffer fills but omits the `tready` backpressure path, a lightly loaded simulation without congestion may miss the defect, whereas traffic bursts that exceed the receiver's service and buffering capacity will overflow the buffer and lose data.[^fn-backpressure-c04] Whether omitting `tready` is actually a bug depends on the interface contract, because a receiver guaranteed to accept every transfer need not provide the signal, and training on additional superficially similar text examples does not establish that a generated bridge satisfies its flow-control obligations. Usable representations must therefore preserve both the circuit structure and the contextual contracts that allow verification tools and reviewers to catch such mistakes before silicon fabrication.

[^fn-backpressure-c04]: **Backpressure**: A mechanism, such as AXI Stream's `tready` signal, that lets a receiver pause upstream transfers. A receiver that cannot always accept arriving traffic needs backpressure or another flow-control arrangement. Without sufficient service, buffering, or flow control, sustained excess arrivals can overflow finite buffers and lose data.

Although representation choice and automation scope are distinct engineering decisions, the chosen representation bounds what an automated loop can observe and change. Because flat token streams do not expose concurrency, clock domains, or physical constraints directly, a workflow that sees only text must either recover those relationships or leave them to downstream checks. A search over a fixed parameter schema requires only the tunable parameters and the template around them, whereas a system proposing coordinated edits across software loop nests, memory hierarchies, and hardware netlists needs intermediate representations that link all three levels to physical feedback.

Compiler frameworks supply that multi-level structure by pairing parameter schemas and control-data flow graphs with typed intermediate representations. The MLIR framework defines modular dialects across abstraction levels, and Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT) applies that infrastructure to hardware design [@CIRCT].[^fn-hardware-ssa-c04] When a flow lowers high-level tensor operations (`linalg`) or affine loop nests (`affine`) into structural hardware dialects (`comb` and `seq`), it must perform explicit high-level synthesis scheduling, resource sharing, and arbitration of memory ports and banks to avoid access conflicts. Static type checks across these dialects can reject malformed transformations and incompatible operands early, while functional correctness and physical realization still require checks that static types cannot express.

[^fn-hardware-ssa-c04]: **Static single assignment (SSA) in hardware IRs**: Software intermediate representations such as LLVM use SSA form, in which each variable is assigned exactly once. In CIRCT's `hw`, `comb`, and `seq` dialects, SSA values represent wires or buses rather than sequential software variables, so single assignment gives every wire one driver. Module bodies are graph regions that do not impose SSA dominance, so cyclic connections can be written; combinational loops are caught by dedicated checking passes rather than by the SSA form itself.

The structural relationships a method must recover become much more demanding as designs grow beyond isolated benchmark modules. Widely used generation benchmarks such as VerilogEval and RTLLM evaluate models mostly on compact leaf modules, whereas production hardware relies on deep module hierarchies, multiple clock domains, and complex bus interfaces. To quantify this structural disparity, a parse of 1,513 SystemVerilog module declarations across six public repositories at pinned commits compares concrete syntax complexity and the depth of source-level module references between benchmark suites and production-oriented RTL (@fig-ch04-ast-complexity-cliff) [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM].
